Video games show both potential cognitive benefits and harms, and current research presents conflicting outcomes rather than a consensus. Experimental and correlational studies report short-term gains in attention, visual processing, executive functions, and problem solving from playing certain video games, especially action or skill-training titles [d1,d4,d5]. Conversely, studies linking excessive or addictive gaming to worse memory, attention, and academic performance suggest potential negative impacts [d2]. Evidence on violent video games indicates limited and mostly short-term negative effects on social-cognitive skills, with some findings even showing improved inhibitory control in adolescents [d3]. Claims about structural brain changes and broad memory deficits are mixed and often rely on low-credibility sources [d6]. Broader discussions acknowledge both cognitive benefits and risks such as addiction and mental health concerns [d7].

Given the mixed evidence base—where benefits are genre- and context-specific and harms are associated with excessive use—there is no single answer to whether video games have a negative impact on cognitive skills.
